title: Psyche and the occasion
short: Psyche ('soul') was a mortal loved by Cupid who became a goddess only late, in Apuleius's Golden Ass; Keats wrote the ode in late April 1819.
body: In Apuleius's second-century tale (Metamorphoses IV-VI), Cupid visits Psyche by night forbidding her to look at him; when she lights a lamp to see him, he flees, and after trials imposed by Venus she is reunited with him and made immortal. Keats knew the story from Adlington's translation and Lemprière's Classical Dictionary, and from Mary Tighe's poem Psyche (1805). In his journal-letter of 30 April 1819 he copied the ode, calling it the first poem over which he had taken even moderate pains, and remarked that Psyche was not embodied as a goddess before Apuleius, so was never worshipped with ancient fervour. It is the first of the great odes of spring 1819.

title: tuneless numbers, wrung / By sweet enforcement
short: 'Numbers' means verses; the modest apology echoes Milton's 'Lycidas', whose opening speaks of 'Bitter constraint, and sad occasion dear'.
body: The formula of the reluctant poet, compelled by an occasion that is both sweet and dear, recalls the opening of 'Lycidas' (1637), with its 'Bitter constraint, and sad occasion dear'; editors note the echo. Keats turns Milton's grief into pleasure: 'sweet enforcement and remembrance dear'. 'Tuneless' is conventional modesty, but it also anticipates the poem's theme, since Psyche has had no hymns, and the poet offers to supply them. The poet also apologises for singing her 'secrets' into her own ear, a playful indiscretion.

title: soft-conched ear
short: Psyche's ear is shaped like a conch shell, soft and curved; the compound is typical of Keats's sensuous coinages.
body: The compound adjective, like 'cool-rooted', 'fragrant-eyed', 'calm-breathing' and 'soft-handed' later in the stanza, condenses an image into a word. 'Conched' suggests both the spiral form of the ear and the sea-shell's power to hold sound. Keats's hyphenated epithets owe something to Spenser and to Chapman's Homer, both formative for him, and hostile reviewers of his earlier volumes mocked such coinages as affected. Here the word also has a point: the poet is singing directly into the goddess's ear, which is shaped to receive sound.

sources.cite: Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats (Longman Annotated English Poets, 1970), 'Ode to Psyche', headnote and notes

anchor: Surely I dreamt to-day, or did I see
title: Surely I dreamt to-day, or did I see
short: The vision is framed by doubt between dream and waking sight, a question Keats returns to at the end of 'Ode to a Nightingale'.
body: The speaker wandered 'thoughtlessly' in a forest and came upon two figures, which he identifies as Cupid and Psyche, sleeping in each other's arms; Psyche has 'awaken'd eyes', perhaps meaning she is now immortal and conscious. The uncertainty of 'dreamt ... or did I see' anticipates the famous ending of 'Ode to a Nightingale' ('Was it a vision, or a waking dream?'). Vendler reads the opening as the poet's discovery of the subject that his own mind will later house, since the seen world becomes the inner sanctuary of the last stanza.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass., 1983), chapter on 'Ode to Psyche'

title: budded Tyrian
short: 'Tyrian' is the deep purple dye of ancient Tyre, used here as a colour noun for purple flowers in bud.
body: Tyre in Phoenicia produced the famous purple dye from the murex shellfish, reserved for royalty in Rome. Keats lists the flowers' colours, 'Blue, silver-white, and budded Tyrian', using the adjective as a noun. The scene, with its 'cool-rooted' flowers and 'whisp'ring roof / Of leaves', is a classical bower in the tradition of Spenser's Bower of Bliss and the bowers of Keats's own Endymion.

title: The winged boy ... His Psyche true
short: The winged boy is Cupid (Eros); the speaker recognises him but has to ask who his companion is, and answers: Psyche, the faithful.
body: Cupid, the son of Venus, is familiar from countless poems and paintings, but Psyche was not traditionally depicted, so the speaker's question 'But who wast thou, O happy, happy dove?' is apt. The dove, Venus's bird, is a term of endearment. 'His Psyche true' stresses her fidelity, the theme of her trials in Apuleius. The lovers' lips 'touch'd not, but had not bade adieu', a poised moment between kisses, like the arrested lovers on the Grecian Urn.

title: At tender eye-dawn of aurorean love
short: 'Aurorean', from Aurora, goddess of dawn, means dawn-like, of the morning; love is at its first awakening, as the lovers wake.
body: The rare adjective is formed from Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn (Greek Eos). Together with 'eye-dawn', it presents waking and new love as one event: the lovers are ready 'past kisses to outnumber' when their eyes open. The phrase links to the myth, in which Psyche's union with Cupid is consummated in darkness, and to the ode's last stanza, which opens a window 'at night' for Love.

anchor: O latest born and loveliest vision far
title: latest born ... Of all Olympus' faded hierarchy
short: Psyche is the youngest and loveliest of the Olympian gods, whose 'faded hierarchy' has lost its worshippers; she came too late to receive cult.
body: The idea comes from Keats's letter: because Psyche was deified only by Apuleius, a writer after the Augustan age, she was never worshipped with the antique fervour of the older gods. The 'faded hierarchy' of Olympus, faded because no longer believed in, contrasts with her loveliness. The poem's argument is that a modern poet, in an age without such faith, can still offer her worship of another kind. The theme of the gods' decline links this ode to Keats's Hyperion, on which he had been working.

title: Phoebe's sapphire-region'd star ... Vesper
short: Psyche is fairer than the moon (Phoebe's 'star', set in a sapphire sky) and than Vesper, the evening star, here a 'glow-worm of the sky'.
body: Phoebe is a name of Diana (Artemis), goddess of the moon; her 'star' is the moon itself in its sapphire region of sky. Vesper (Hesperus) is Venus as the evening star, whimsically called an 'amorous glow-worm', perhaps because the female glow-worm shines to attract a mate. Both are older deities with their own cults, against whom Psyche, 'temple thou hast none', is set.

anchor: No voice, no lute, no pipe, no incense sweet
title: No voice, no lute ... Thy voice, thy lute
short: The list of all the worship Psyche lacks is repeated in stanza 3 with 'thy' for 'no': the poet will himself supply each element of cult.
body: The negative catalogue (no temple, altar, virgin-choir, voice, lute, pipe, incense, shrine, grove, oracle, prophet) is answered word for word after the poet's resolution 'So let me be thy choir'. The device turns rhetorical absence into presence and dramatises the poem's claim that poetry can make up for lost religion. The 'pale-mouth'd prophet dreaming' is the oracle-priest in trance, like the Pythia at Delphi; 'chain-swung censer' (later 'swinged censer') is the swung incense-burner of temple worship. Vendler analyses the ode's structure around this repetition.

anchor: Too, too late for the fond believing lyre
title: fond believing lyre
short: 'Fond' means foolishly credulous as well as loving: the lyre of ancient poets who believed in the gods; the modern poet comes too late.
body: The stanza recalls a time 'When holy were the haunted forest boughs, / Holy the air, the water, and the fire', a world in which every element had its divinity, before 'these days so far retir'd / From happy pieties'. The older sense of 'fond' (OED: foolish, credulous) sits alongside the modern 'affectionate'. Keats does not lament simply; he sees, and sings, 'by my own eyes inspired', an assertion of a poetry grounded in the individual imagination rather than inherited belief. The passage is often compared with Wordsworth's sonnet 'The world is too much with us'.

title: thy lucent fans, / Fluttering among the faint Olympians
short: Psyche's 'lucent fans' are her shining wings, butterfly-like, since psyche in Greek also means butterfly.
body: 'Lucent' (Latin lucens) means shining or translucent. In ancient art Psyche was often shown with butterfly wings, the butterfly being an emblem of the soul emerging from the body as from a chrysalis; Keats's 'winged Psyche' (l. 6) and 'fans' recall that iconography. The 'faint Olympians' are the faded gods of stanza 2, through whom she flutters as the newest and brightest.

title: build a fane / In some untrodden region of my mind
short: The poet will build Psyche's temple in his own mind: the ode turns from outer worship to an inner sanctuary of imagination.
body: A 'fane' is a temple. The final stanza internalises the cult: the temple is in 'some untrodden region of my mind', the pines of its grove are 'branched thoughts, new grown with pleasant pain', and its landscape of mountains, Dryads and zephyrs is mental. Keats had written in a letter of May 1818 of the mind as a 'Mansion of Many Apartments', and the stanza works out that conceit. Critics debate whether the inner temple is a triumph of imagination over lost faith, as Vendler argues, or a retreat into solitude that the later odes question.

title: Fledge
short: To 'fledge' is to cover with feathers; the dark trees will feather the mountain ridges, a bold verb for a forest seen from afar.
body: The verb usually describes a young bird growing its feathers. Applied to trees on mountains it suggests both the feathery look of distant pines and the new growth of thought ('new grown with pleasant pain'). Keats's landscape here is sublime but inward, with 'wild-ridged mountains steep by steep', where the 'moss-lain Dryads', tree nymphs, are lulled to sleep.

title: the gardener Fancy ... will never breed the same
short: Fancy, the inventive faculty, is a gardener whose crossbreeding produces endless new flowers, each different.
body: 'Fancy' for Keats is the playful, image-making imagination (compare his poem 'Fancy', 1818), not yet sharply distinguished from imagination as Coleridge distinguished them. The 'wreath'd trellis of a working brain' supports flowers 'without a name', unlike any in nature, and the gardener 'will never breed the same', a phrase that suggests both endless variety and the impossibility of exact repetition. Some critics find a note of unease here: the sanctuary is made of 'shadowy thought', and what the mind breeds is unreal.

anchor: A bright torch, and a casement ope at night
title: A bright torch, and a casement ope at night, / To let the warm Love in
short: The ending reverses Apuleius: there Psyche's lamp drove Cupid away; here a torch and an open window welcome Love in.
body: In the myth Cupid comes to Psyche only in darkness; when she lights a lamp to look at him, a drop of hot oil wakes him and he flees. Keats's final image offers both light and an open casement, so that Love can come and be seen. 'Warm Love' is Cupid, but the lines also suggest the warmth of human love in a poem written during Keats's love for Fanny Brawne. The open window, letting the outside in, slightly qualifies the self-enclosed mental sanctuary: the shrine of thought waits for something it cannot produce itself.

anchor: So let me be thy choir, and make a moan
title: Form
short: An irregular ode of four stanzas of unequal length, mainly pentameter with shorter lines, and varied rhyme; it led to the regular stanzas of the later odes.
body: Keats's letter says the ode was written with care, in a period when he was experimenting with stanza forms; the same letter contains his sonnet 'If by dull rhymes our English must be chain'd', which expresses dissatisfaction with the sonnet's fixed schemes. 'Psyche' combines sonnet-like quatrains and couplets in irregular stanzas with short lines interspersed. Critics such as Stillinger and Vendler see it as the experimental first of the odes; the following odes ('Nightingale', 'Grecian Urn', 'Melancholy') use a regular ten-line stanza derived from the sonnet.
